ai.literal: Folly that-which-is-called one-thing what if-asked, harm having-taken profit to-go letting.
ai.translation: If asked what the one thing called folly is, it is grasping what causes harm and letting go of what brings profit.
ai.modern: பேதைமை என்று சொல்லப்படுவது என்னவென்றால், தனக்குத் துன்பம் தருவதைப் பற்றிக்கொண்டு, நன்மை தருவதைக் கைவிடுவதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the core nature of folly or ignorance. The poet asks what the single defining trait of folly is, and answers by contrasting 'ētam' (harm) with 'ūtiyam' (profit or benefit). A foolish person actively grasps and holds onto things that cause them harm, while carelessly letting go of things that would bring them true benefit. Thus, folly is shown not merely as a lack of knowledge, but as an actively destructive pattern of choices.

ai.literal: Among follies all, folly is desire for proper-not in-oneself doing.
ai.translation: The greatest folly among all follies is to love doing things that are unfitting for oneself.
ai.modern: எல்லாப் பேதைமைகளிலும் பெரிய பேதைமை, தனக்குப் பொருந்தாத செயல்களைச் செய்வதில் விருப்பம் கொள்வதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the ultimate form of foolishness. While there are many kinds of folly, the worst is having a desire to engage in actions that are improper or unfitting for one's position. The word 'kai' here means proper conduct or fitness, and 'kai alla' refers to things that are not proper. By loving and doing such unfitting things, a person brings about their own ruin, making it the greatest folly.

ai.literal: Shamelessness, not investigating, affection's absence, anything even one not cherishing: fool's deed.
ai.translation: Shamelessness, lack of inquiry, absence of affection, and failing to cherish anything whatsoever are the defining actions of a fool.
ai.modern: வெட்கப்பட வேண்டியதற்கு வெட்கப்படாமை, ஆராய வேண்டியதை ஆராயாமை, யார் மாட்டும் அன்பு இல்லாமை, எதையும் பாதுகாக்காமை ஆகியவையே அறிவிலியின் செயல்களாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet lists four negative traits that characterize a foolish person. First is shamelessness, meaning they do not feel ashamed of disgraceful acts. Second is the failure to investigate or seek out what is good. Third is a complete lack of affection or human connection. Finally, they fail to cherish or protect anything of value, making these destructive habits the true mark of ignorance.

ai.literal: Having read, even having understood, and having taught to others, oneself not submitting than the fool fools there are not.
ai.translation: There are no greater fools than the fool who reads, understands, and teaches others, yet fails to control his own conduct.
ai.modern: நூல்களைப் படித்து, அவற்றின் பொருளை உணர்ந்து, மற்றவர்களுக்கும் எடுத்துச் சொல்லியும், தான் அந்த நெறிப்படி நடக்காத முட்டாளை விடப் பெரிய முட்டாள்கள் யாருமில்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the ultimate form of folly. It describes a person who has read widely, understood the meaning of what they read, and even teaches those principles to others. However, if they fail to apply that knowledge to control their own behavior, their learning is useless. The word 'aṭaṅkā' means not submitting or not controlling oneself, showing that true wisdom requires living by what one knows, and lacking this makes one the greatest fool.

ai.literal: One birth deed performs fool, all seven births himself having entered will sink hell.
ai.translation: In a single birth, a fool performs deeds that will plunge him into hell, where he will sink and suffer for seven births.
ai.modern: ஒரு பிறவியில் செய்யும் தீய செயல்களால், அறிவற்றவன் தொடர்ந்து வரும் ஏழு பிறவிகளிலும் நரகத்தில் புகுந்து துன்பத்தில் அழுந்துவான்.
ai.explanation: The couplet contrasts the brevity of a fool's actions with the lasting consequences they bring. 'ஒருமை' (one birth) and 'எழுமை' (seven births) are juxtaposed to show how a single lifetime of foolish deeds leads to prolonged suffering. The word 'அளறு' refers to hell or a deep mire, illustrating the inescapable misery the fool creates for himself. By acting without foresight, the fool ensures his own downfall across multiple lifetimes.

ai.literal: Failure will happen or, fetters will wear, method not-knowing fool task if undertakes.
ai.translation: If a fool who does not know the proper method undertakes a task, either the task will fail or he will end up in fetters.
ai.modern: செயல்முறையை அறியாத பேதை ஒரு செயலைச் செய்யத் தொடங்கினால், அச்செயல் பழுதாகும் அல்லது அவன் விலங்கு பூட்டப்படுவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns of the dangers when an ignorant person takes charge of a task. The word 'kai' here refers to the proper method or conduct required for an action. If a fool attempts a task without knowing how to execute it, two outcomes are possible. Either the task itself will end in failure ('poy'), or his blunders will be so severe that he will be punished and put in fetters. While 'punai' can mean an ornament, in this context of a fool's failure, it is best understood as fetters or chains.

ai.literal: Strangers to eat fully, relatives will starve, a fool great wealth when attained.
ai.translation: When a fool attains great wealth, strangers will eat their fill while his own relatives starve.
ai.modern: ஒரு அறிவிலி பெருஞ்செல்வத்தை அடைந்தால், அவனுக்குத் தொடர்பில்லாத அயலார் வயிறார உண்பார்கள்; ஆனால் அவனுடைய உறவினர்கள் பசியால் வாடுவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet illustrates the misplaced priorities of a foolish person who acquires wealth. Instead of supporting their own family and relatives, a fool squanders their resources on strangers who might simply flatter them. The sharp contrast between strangers eating fully and relatives starving highlights the fool's complete lack of judgment and moral responsibility.

ai.literal: Madness one-man like-having-intoxicated indeed fool his hand some wealth if-gets.
ai.translation: If a fool gets hold of some wealth in his hands, it is like a madman becoming intoxicated.
ai.modern: ஒரு பேதை தன் கையில் ஒரு செல்வத்தைப் பெற்றால், அது ஏற்கெனவே பைத்தியம் பிடித்த ஒருவன் மது குடித்து வெறித்தது போன்றதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares a fool acquiring wealth to a madman getting drunk. The word 'maiyal' means madness or delusion, and 'kalittarru' refers to the state of being intoxicated. Just as alcohol worsens the erratic behavior of someone who is already mad, sudden wealth amplifies the harmful and unpredictable actions of a fool.

ai.literal: Greatly sweet is fools' friendship; at separation, pain-giving thing, there is not one.
ai.translation: The friendship of fools is highly pleasant, for when it ends, it leaves behind no pain at all.
ai.modern: அறிவில்லாதவர்களுடன் கொள்ளும் நட்பு மிகவும் இனிமையானது; ஏனெனில், அவர்களைப் பிரியும்போது நமக்கு எந்தத் துன்பமும் ஏற்படுவதில்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses deep irony to describe the nature of associating with foolish people. It states that the friendship of fools is exceedingly sweet. The reason for this sweetness is revealed in the second line: when the friendship ends, it causes absolutely no pain or sorrow. Unlike true friendship, which brings immense grief upon separation, parting from a fool brings only relief. The word 'கேண்மை' denotes friendship, while 'பீழை' means distress, highlighting the contrast between the expected sorrow of parting and the actual relief felt when a fool leaves.

ai.literal: Unwashed foot inside bed having placed it is like, noble ones' in assembly fool entering.
ai.translation: A fool entering an assembly of the wise is like placing unwashed feet onto a clean bed.
ai.modern: சான்றோர்களின் அவைக்குள் ஒரு அறிவிலி நுழைவது, கழுவாத கால்களுடன் படுக்கையில் ஏறுவதற்கு ஒப்பாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a vivid, everyday simile to illustrate the disruptive nature of ignorance. The phrase "கழாஅ கால்" (unwashed feet) placed into "பள்ளியுள்" (a bed) evokes the spoiling of a clean, restful place with dirt. In the same way, the entry ("புகல்") of a fool ("பேதை") into a gathering of noble, wise people ("சான்றோர் குழாஅத்து") pollutes the refined and harmonious environment of the assembly. The poet shows that ignorance is not merely an absence of knowledge, but an active stain on a cultured space.
